columns/many: Multiplying two matrices, A and B, is written A B, and it is many matrix-vector products at once. A multiplies each column of B, and each answer becomes a column of the result.
columns/inner: So each column of B must be as long as a row of A: A's columns must equal B's rows. These are the inner dimensions, three and three.
columns/outer: The result keeps the outer ones: A's two rows, and B's four columns. Two by three, times three by four, gives two by four.
columns/rule: In general, for any sizes m, n and k, m by n, times n by k, gives m by k. The inner n's must match, and they disappear.
columns/chain: A chain of three goes two at a time. Take a third matrix, C, four by five. A B is two by four, and two by four, times four by five, gives two by five.
order/swap: Order matters. B times A is three by four, times two by three: the inner dimensions are four and two, so there is no product.
order/pair: Now take A, two by three, and a new matrix M, two by four. A times M fails too: its inner dimensions are three and two.
order/fix: Transposing A swaps its shape to three by two. Three by two, times two by four, gives three by four.
order/flip: M transpose times A works as well, and lays the same numbers out the other way: four by three.
